strengths: A rigorous theoretical derivation (Proposition 3.1) shows how to compute the otherwise intractable distillation objective for ResShift using an auxiliary 'fake' ResShift model, with a full proof in the appendix and clear discussion of why direct backpropagation is infeasible.

Extensive relation to prior distillation methods (VSD, SiD, FGM, IBMD, AddSR/ADD/SDS) is provided in the appendix, including derivations showing RSD reduces to or differs from these losses, which situates the contribution well within the literature and clarifies what is genuinely new (joint- vs marginal-distribution matching).

Thorough empirical evaluation across multiple protocols (SinSR-style and OSEDiff-style), multiple real-world and synthetic datasets (RealSR, RealSet65, DRealSR, ImageNet-Test, DIV2K), and many metrics (fidelity and no-reference perceptual), consistently showing RSD outperforms its closest 1-step competitor SinSR by a large margin while being far more parameter/memory-efficient than T2I-based diffusion SR models (OSEDiff, SUPIR).

Useful ablations isolating the effect of multistep training (N) and of the added supervised losses (LPIPS, GAN), and a controlled comparison against a self-implemented VSD baseline adapted to ResShift (ResShift-VSD) and against AddSR, strengthening the causal claims about design choices.

Honest limitations/failure-case section (Appendix H) with concrete visual failure examples (anime image, texture-rich scenes, small-detail hallucination) rather than only favorable qualitative comparisons, plus a reasonable discussion of societal impact.

Good reproducibility support: training hyperparameters, compute budget, dataset/license tables, and baseline checkpoints/repositories are all documented in appendices C and provided training/inference time comparisons (Table 4, Appendix C).
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the overall recipe (auxiliary 'fake' diffusion model + distillation + GAN/LPIPS losses) closely follows DMD2/VSD-style one-step distillation; the main new element is a ResShift-specific tractable reformulation and a claim that joint-trajectory matching is preferable to per-timestep marginal matching, but this superiority is argued heuristically/intuitively (Appendix A.1) rather than proven, since both objectives should share the same global optimum under exact optimization.

Several key comparison tables (Tables 12, 13, 14, and portions of Table 11) borrow numbers directly from other papers (SinSR, OSEDiff) rather than re-running them in the authors' own pipeline, which can introduce inconsistencies in evaluation protocol/metric implementation and complicates claims of a fully controlled, fair comparison.

Performance relative to T2I-based SOTA (OSEDiff, SUPIR) is mixed rather than uniformly favorable (e.g., worse CLIPIQA than SUPIR on synthetic data, worse than OSEDiff on some perceptual metrics in Table 3/13), so the 'competitive with SOTA T2I methods' claim is only partially supported and is acknowledged with some hedging in the text.

The method's quality is explicitly capped by the teacher ResShift model's weaker generative prior compared to large-scale T2I priors; the higher-resolution training experiment (Appendix E) shows only modest gains, indicating limited headroom/scalability of the approach without a stronger teacher.

No variance/error bars or multiple training runs are reported for the main results or ablations, making it hard to assess whether some of the smaller reported differences (e.g., in Table 5/6 ablations) are statistically meaningful.

The unexplained result that RSD's inference time is lower than SinSR's despite both being 1-step methods with similar-sized architectures (Table 4) is not discussed, leaving a minor unexplained discrepancy in the efficiency claims.

strengths: The paper provides a careful theoretical derivation (Proposition 3.1) that converts an otherwise intractable bilevel distillation objective for ResShift into a tractable 'fake-model' formulation, and the appendix offers an unusually thorough discussion relating this loss to VSD, SiD, FGM and IBMD, including full derivations (Appendix A) and explicit gradient-level comparisons.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple real-world (RealSR, RealSet65, DRealSR) and synthetic (ImageNet-Test, DIV2K) benchmarks, under two different protocols borrowed from SinSR and OSEDiff, with additional baselines (GAN-, transformer-, T2I-based) reported in the appendix (Tables 10-13).

Clear and consistent improvement over the most direct competitor, SinSR, on nearly all perceptual metrics (LPIPS, CLIPIQA, MUSIQ, DISTS, NIQE, MANIQA) while maintaining competitive fidelity (PSNR/SSIM), supporting the central claim that RSD improves upon prior ResShift distillation.

Strong attention to computational efficiency: RSD has ~10x fewer parameters and far less GPU memory/inference time than T2I-based SR models (Table 4), which is a practically relevant contribution for real-time deployment.

Good reproducibility practices: detailed hyperparameters, training time, dataset/baseline licensing tables (Appendix C), full pseudocode (Appendix B), and an honest limitations/failure-case section with visual examples (Appendix H) including cases where the teacher itself fails or the method hallucinates/blurs.
Ablation studies (multistep timestep count, effect of supervised losses) are included and reasonably informative (Tables 5-6).
weaknesses: The core technical idea (training an auxiliary 'fake' diffusion model to approximate the student-induced distribution and matching it against a frozen teacher, à la DMD2/SiD/VSD) is not new in itself; the contribution is primarily its careful adaptation/derivation for the ResShift residual-shifting process. While the authors argue this adaptation is nontrivial, the overall novelty is incremental relative to the broader one-step diffusion distillation literature, and the paper's own appendix shows the final loss can be algebraically rewritten to closely resemble SiD/FGM objectives (Appendix A.2).

Results relative to SOTA T2I-based methods (OSEDiff, SUPIR) are mixed rather than uniformly favorable: RSD trails on CLIPIQA in multiple tables (Tables 1-3, 11-13) and the paper itself notes a confound (RSD trained on 256x256 crops vs. OSEDiff's 512x512 crops) that biases comparisons in OSEDiff's favor; when this is controlled for in Appendix E, RSD still underperforms ResShift/SinSR on PSNR/SSIM and does not clearly surpass SinSR except on no-reference metrics.

The abstract's claim that RSD 'outperforms the teacher model by a large margin' is only true for a subset of perceptual no-reference metrics; fidelity metrics (PSNR/SSIM) are frequently worse than the teacher ResShift across Tables 1-3, which somewhat overstates the generality of the improvement.

No variance/uncertainty is reported for any metric (single-run point estimates throughout), which is a common but notable gap given several comparisons are close (e.g., RSD vs. SinSR PSNR/SSIM in Table 1-3, RSD vs. OSEDiff MUSIQ in several tables).

Failure case analysis (Appendix H, Figures 6-8) shows RSD inherits most of the limitations of the ResShift teacher (blurring, inability to hallucinate fine details, poor performance on cluttered/small-detail regions), underscoring that gains are bounded by—and somewhat marginal relative to—the teacher's own capacity, which tempers the significance of the contribution.

The paper is very dense with notation-heavy derivations across the main text and an 11-section, 43-page appendix; while thorough, this heavy formalism (much of which re-derives known distillation losses) could have been condensed, and the core practical takeaways are sometimes diluted by the volume of auxiliary theoretical comparisons.

strengths: The paper derives a tractable distillation objective (Proposition 3.1) for one-step ResShift distillation using an auxiliary 'fake' ResShift model, with a thorough theoretical treatment that clearly relates the proposed RSD loss to existing fake-model-based distillation approaches (VSD, SiD, FGM, IBMD) in an extensive appendix, showing the loss corresponds to matching the joint distribution over the full trajectory rather than only marginals as in VSD.

Experiments are extensive: evaluation spans multiple real-world (RealSR, RealSet65, DRealSR) and synthetic (ImageNet-Test, DIV2K) benchmarks, with both SinSR-style and OSEDiff-style evaluation protocols, many additional baselines in the appendix (GAN-based, transformer-based, T2I-based SR), and ablations on multistep training and supervised losses.

RSD achieves meaningful efficiency gains: ~5x less GPU memory and ~10x fewer parameters than T2I-based SR models (OSEDiff, SUPIR) while matching or exceeding SinSR, and training converges roughly 3x faster than SinSR, which is a practically relevant contribution for real-time SR deployment.

The paper includes a reasonably transparent and honest limitations section with concrete failure cases (bicubic-like outputs, hallucinations under severe degradation, poor performance on small/background details) and a reasonable discussion of societal impact, rather than hiding method weaknesses.

Reproducibility details are good: datasets, licenses, baseline checkpoints/URLs, training hyperparameters, and pseudocode (Algorithms 1-2) are all provided in appendices, making the work relatively easy to replicate.
weaknesses: The empirical superiority of RSD is metric-dependent and often marginal rather than a clear 'large margin' as claimed in the abstract/intro: across Tables 1-3 and the extended tables in Appendix D, RSD is frequently only second-best, loses to SUPIR/OSEDiff on CLIPIQA, and sometimes loses to ResShift/SinSR on fidelity metrics (PSNR/SSIM), undercutting the strength of the headline claims.

All perceptual evaluation relies solely on no-reference metrics (CLIPIQA, MUSIQ, NIQE, MANIQA) and reference metrics (PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS); there is no human preference study, despite the introduction explicitly motivating the work by citing human-evaluation findings favoring diffusion SR models over GANs, which is an inconsistency between the motivation and the evaluation methodology actually used.

The theoretical justification in Section 3.2 (Eq. 6) that matching the fake-model prediction to the teacher implies the generator's distribution approximates the data distribution is presented as a motivating assumption rather than a proven guarantee; no convergence or consistency analysis is given for the 2-player (generator/fake-model) optimization, which is known to be unstable in GAN-like settings.

The core methodological novelty is incremental: the paper's own appendix derivations show that the proposed loss is algebraically very close to existing fake-score distillation objectives (SiD, FGM, VSD, IBMD) up to sign/weighting choices, so the main contribution is largely the application/adaptation of known distillation machinery to the ResShift SR backbone rather than a fundamentally new principle.

The method's performance ceiling is explicitly bounded by the ResShift teacher's quality (acknowledged in Appendix E, where RSD trained at 512x512 still underperforms OSEDiff on no-reference metrics), and no experiments demonstrate RSD generalizing to other DDPM-based SR teachers despite claims that the method applies broadly to any DDPM-framework diffusion SR model.

Presentation is dense with heavy notation and many cross-referenced equations/propositions spread across a long appendix, which may hinder readability and independent verification by readers not deeply familiar with the ResShift/VSD/DMD2 literature.
